summary:
Małopolska adopted a voivodeship-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under EU funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the eastern belt. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the voivodeship's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, Kraków—the capital and Poland's second city—has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 newly elected mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced he would become the first Kraków mayor ever to attend the city's LGBT Equality March and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor Jacek Majchrowski (2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in Kraków's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed voivodeship document.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52: the resolution history pulls it down, Kraków's positive trajectory prevents a deeper drop. Above Lublin (0.45), where no equivalent capital-city counter-signal exists, and well above Subcarpathian (0.42), where the capital actively banned a march. Below Masovian (0.56), where Warsaw's institutional machinery works continuously in the visitor's favour.

sources.summary: LGBTQ+ news report (September 2021): Malopolska voivodeship was among the regional authorities repealing their 'LGBT-free' resolutions on 20 September 2021 after the European Commission threatened regional development funding; the article situates the repeals in the wider pattern of roughly 100 municipalities adopting and later withdrawing anti-LGBT declarations.

Legal-overview article on the rise and fall of Poland's LGBT-free zones: between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 local governments adopted 'LGBT ideology'-free resolutions or Ordo Iuris-drafted family-rights charters covering roughly a third of the country at peak; the documents created no criminal penalties but symbolically sidelined LGBT residents from civic life; the national human-rights commissioner's litigation led courts to strike them down as unconstitutional, the EU threatened to freeze billions in regional funds, and the last remaining zone was abolished in spring 2025.

tangentialFactors: Both poles - the repealed voivodeship resolution and the capital mayor's march attendance - concern LGBT public presence broadly rather than trans status specifically; they set the general institutional climate a trans visitor reads locally, without trans-specific enforcement either way.
